title: The Essence and the Energies
subtitle: God is unknowable in his essence and truly given in his energies, and both are wholly God.
summary: If God's will is numerically the same reality as his eternal and unchangeable essence, then the act by which he wills this world is as necessary as he is, and creation stops being a gift. The Orthodox answer distinguishes the essence, which no creature will ever grasp, from the uncreated energies, in which God genuinely gives himself, without dividing God into parts. Built on St Basil's Letters 234 and 235, with Irenaeus, Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory the Theologian, Cyril of Jerusalem, John Chrysostom and John of Damascus.
origin: Discord, dogma-exegesis: God, Necessity, and Metaphysical Dead Ends: Why the Essence-Energies Distinction is Non-Negotiable.

essay.text: Ask whether God can be known and two answers come back, and both of them sound pious. The first says that God is past finding out, so whatever reaches us is a report about him and never him. The second says that God gives himself, really and without reserve, so that a person praying in a cold church is not being informed about God but is being given God. Orthodox theology holds both, and the distinction between the divine essence and the divine energies is how it holds them. This is not a technicality for specialists. It decides whether the apostle's promise that we may be partakers of the divine nature describes something that actually happens to a human being, or is a figure of speech for something else that happens instead.
The problem: a God who could not have done otherwise

Begin with the objection that makes the distinction necessary, because it is the reason the question is not merely verbal. The classical scholastic account of divine simplicity, worked out with great care in the Latin tradition and most famously by Thomas Aquinas, holds that there is no composition of any kind in God. His essence, his existence, his knowledge, his power and his will are not distinct realities in him but one identical reality, distinguished in our speech and not in him. Now set two confessions beside that. God's essence is eternal and unchangeable. And God created freely, so that there might have been no world at all. If the act by which God wills this world is numerically the same reality as the essence, then that act is as eternal and as unchangeable as the essence is, and it becomes very hard to say in what sense the world might not have been. Creation begins to look as necessary as God. Nobody on either side wants that conclusion. The Latin answer is that God's willing is one eternal act, that he wills his own goodness necessarily and everything else freely, and that the contingency belongs to what is willed rather than to the willing. That answer deserves to be stated in its own terms rather than caricatured, and many careful people find it sufficient. The Orthodox reply is that it asserts the freedom rather than accounting for it. If the willing simply is the essence, and the essence could not have been otherwise, then saying that its object could have been otherwise restates the problem instead of solving it. This is a real disagreement between Christians, not a misunderstanding, and it is worth keeping the temperature low while we work on it.

St Basil the Great wrote Letters 234 and 235 to St Amphilochius of Iconium against a party who taught that the human mind can lay hold of the very essence of God, since unbegottenness names that essence and is perfectly intelligible. Their challenge was blunt. Do you worship what you know, or what you do not know? Basil's answer set the terms the Church has used ever since. We know God's greatness, his power, his wisdom, his goodness, his providence over us and the justness of his judgment. We do not know his essence. Then comes the sentence this study is built on: the operations are various, and the essence simple, and we know our God from his operations, while his essence remains beyond our reach. The Greek word behind operations is energeia. The nineteenth-century translators render it operations or workings, later English renders it energies, and it is the same word, so a reader meeting energies for the first time should not hear anything electrical in it. Notice also what Basil does not say. He does not say that we know nothing. He says he knows what is knowable of God and knows what lies beyond his comprehension, and that the disciples came to worship by a knowledge that reached them through the operations they saw.
The energies are God himself, not a message about God

The next step is the one everything depends on. The energies are not creatures. They are not effects standing between us and God like a screen, and they are not information delivered on his behalf. They are God going forth, God as he gives himself, so that what a creature receives in grace is God and not a created substitute. St Gregory of Nyssa says that every operation which extends from God to the creation has its origin from the Father, proceeds through the Son and is perfected in the Holy Spirit, one operation of the one God and not three. St Gregory the Theologian, having gone up the mountain to lay hold on God, reports that what he saw was not the first and unmingled Nature but the Majesty, the Glory that is manifested among the creatures. St Basil, listing what the Holy Spirit works in a soul that has been cleansed, ends the list with the being made God. This is why the distinction belongs to prayer and not only to argument. The light the apostles saw on Tabor was not a created glare produced for the occasion, and the grace given in the mysteries is not a parcel sent by a God who stays at home.
But does this not put parts in God?

This is the strongest thing said on the other side, and it should be given its full force. If the essence and the energies are really distinct, and both of them are God, then there appear to be two realities in God rather than one. Whatever has two realities in it is composite. A composite depends on its parts and on whatever holds them together, so it cannot be the first cause. On that reading the distinction buys a knowable God at the price of the God of Nicaea. The Orthodox answer begins by asking what composition actually means. Parts are prior to the whole they make, each is less than the whole, they can in principle be taken apart, and something must put them together. None of that holds here. The energies are not pieces of God laid alongside another piece called the essence. Each energy is the whole God acting, wholly present, not a portion of him allotted to a task, and the sun's light is not a slice of the sun sent out on errands. The Church already speaks this way elsewhere without anyone alleging composition. The Father is not the Son, and God is not thereby divided. God's mercy is not his justice, and God is not thereby assembled out of virtues. St John of Damascus makes exactly this move: he says the Deity is simple and uncompound, refuses to treat uncreatedness, goodness, everlastingness and the rest as essential differences that would compound God, and says that each affirmation about God signifies not what he is in essence but a relation, or something that follows the nature, or an energy. What is genuinely at stake, then, is not whether God is simple, since both sides confess that he is. It is what simplicity requires. Orthodox theology denies that it requires collapsing everything in God into a single undifferentiated point, and holds that the difference between God as he is in himself and God as he freely gives himself is one we find rather than one we invent. St Gregory Palamas states this most exactly, and his argument is described here rather than quoted, because the standard English of the 150 Chapters and of the Triads is modern and under copyright. In substance he holds that the energies are neither the essence nor accidents, since they neither come into being nor pass away; that essence and energy are identical in one respect and distinct in another; that God is wholly present in each of his energies; and that this no more divides God than the distinction of the three Persons divides him. The councils of Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 received that teaching, and it stands in the Synodikon of Orthodoxy. A Catholic reader may answer that all of this can be carried by a distinction of reason with a foundation in the thing itself, and where that answer is made in earnest the distance between us narrows a good deal. It is only honest to say so.
Creation is a gift, and so is deification

Now come back to where we started. St John of Damascus draws the line the argument needed. Begetting in God is the work of nature and comes out of his own essence, and is therefore without beginning and everlasting, while creation is the work of will, and is therefore not co-eternal with God. St Athanasius had already put it as plainly as it can be put: a man by counsel builds a house, but by nature he begets a son. The Son is not a work of will. The world is. So the world does not rest on a necessity inside God. It rests on a free act, which is the only ground on which it can be called a gift, and the only ground on which thanksgiving means anything. And the same distinction that keeps creation free keeps communion real. Because the essence is beyond every creature, no man has seen God at any time, and none ever will. Because the energies are God himself, blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. The Church has never had to choose between those two sentences, and this is the reason why.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.text: But in respect to His greatness, and His wonderful glory, no man shall see God and live, for the Father is incomprehensible; but in regard to His love, and kindness, and as to His infinite power, even this He grants to those who love Him, that is, to see God, which thing the prophets did also predict.
florilegium.gloss: Two centuries before the controversy has a vocabulary, Irenaeus already draws the line in the right place. As to his greatness God cannot be seen; as to his love, his kindness and his power he can be, and is. That is the distinction, stated as a pastoral fact rather than as a theory.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.text: For as those who see the light are within the light, and partake of its brilliancy; even so, those who see God are in God, and receive of His splendour. But His splendour vivifies them; those, therefore, who see God, do receive life.
florilegium.gloss: The vision is not a look from outside. To see God is to be inside what is seen and to receive of it, and what is received gives life. This is participation described before anyone had to defend it.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: If they say that essence is something distinct, let them not put us in the wrong on the score of simplicity. For they confess themselves that there is a distinction between the essence and each one of the attributes enumerated. The operations are various, and the essence simple, but we say that we know our God from His operations, but do not undertake to approach near to His essence. His operations come down to us, but His essence remains beyond our reach.
florilegium.gloss: The anchor text of the whole doctrine, and note that Basil meets the charge of compromising simplicity in the same breath in which he makes the distinction. The word rendered operations is energeiai. Basil's opponents had argued exactly what is argued now, that since God is simple, whatever we know of him must be his essence.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: So knowledge of the divine essence involves perception of His incomprehensibility, and the object of our worship is not that of which we comprehend the essence, but of which we comprehend that the essence exists.
florilegium.gloss: Basil's answer to the taunt that a God whose essence is unknown is an unknown God. To know the essence rightly is to know that it cannot be compassed, and worship is directed to the God who is, not to a definition of what he is.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: When did the disciples worship Him? Was it not when they saw creation subject to Him? It was from the obedience of sea and winds to Him that they recognised His Godhead. Therefore the knowledge came from the operations, and the worship from the knowledge.
florilegium.gloss: The order Basil sets out is operations, then knowledge, then worship. The disciples in the boat did not begin from a definition of the divine essence. They saw an operation and worshipped.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: Yes; but I at the same time both know and do not know Timothy, though not in the same way and in the same degree. It is not that I do not know in the same way in which I do know; but I know in one way and am ignorant in one way. I know him according to his form and other properties; but I am ignorant of his essence.
florilegium.gloss: The homeliest illustration in the whole dispute, and the most useful. Knowing and not knowing the same person, in different respects, is ordinary human experience and involves no contradiction. Basil is showing that the grammar he uses of God is not a special pleading invented for the occasion.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: The divine nature, on the other hand, in all the words which are contrived, remains always inexplicable, as I always teach. We have learned that it is beneficent, judicial, righteous, good, and so on; and so have been taught differences of operations. But we are, nevertheless, unable to understand the nature of the operator through our idea of the operations.
florilegium.gloss: The rule stated in both directions. The differences among the operations are real and instructive, and they still do not deliver the nature of the one who operates. NPNF prints this letter among St Basil's; many scholars assign it to St Gregory of Nyssa, and the argument is the same in either hand.

florilegium.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
florilegium.text: Hence it is clear that by any of the terms we use the Divine nature itself is not signified, but some one of its surroundings is made known. For we say, it may be, that the Deity is incorruptible, or powerful, or whatever else we are accustomed to say of Him. But in each of these terms we find a peculiar sense, fit to be understood or asserted of the Divine nature, yet not expressing that which that nature is in its essence.
florilegium.gloss: The Greek behind surroundings is ta peri auton, the things around him. Nyssa's point is not that our words are false but that they land somewhere other than the essence, and that they land on something real when they land.

florilegium.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
florilegium.text: But in the case of the Divine nature we do not similarly learn that the Father does anything by Himself in which the Son does not work conjointly, or again that the Son has any special operation apart from the Holy Spirit; but every operation which extends from God to the Creation, and is named according to our variable conceptions of it, has its origin from the Father, and proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit.
florilegium.gloss: The unity of the divine operation, and the reason the Fathers can speak of many energies without speaking of many Gods. One operation goes out from the Father through the Son and is completed in the Spirit, and it is named variously by us according to what we can take in.

florilegium.author: St Gregory Nazianzen
florilegium.text: not That which abides within the first veil, and is hidden by the Cherubim; but only that Nature, which at last even reaches to us. And that is, as far as I can learn, the Majesty, or as holy David calls it, the Glory which is manifested among the creatures, which It has produced and governs. For these are the Back Parts of God, which He leaves behind Him, as tokens of Himself like the shadows and reflection of the sun in the water, which show the sun to our weak eyes, because we cannot look at the sun himself, for by his unmixed light he is too strong for our power of perception.
florilegium.gloss: The Theologian climbs the mountain to lay hold on God and comes back describing what Moses was given, the back parts. What reaches us is the Majesty and the Glory, which is God manifested among the creatures, and not a creature standing in for him.

florilegium.author: St Cyril of Jerusalem
florilegium.text: For of God we speak not all we ought (for that is known to Him only), but so much as the capacity of human nature has received, and so much as our weakness can bear. For we explain not what God is but candidly confess that we have not exact knowledge concerning Him. For in what concerns God to confess our ignorance is the best knowledge.
florilegium.gloss: Said not to a synod but to catechumens preparing for baptism, which is where the doctrine belongs. Confessing that we cannot explain what God is is presented as the beginning of knowledge and not the end of it.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
florilegium.text: our argument is God, whom it is impossible to describe, or to imagine worthily; hence this man nowhere assigns the name of His essence, (for it is not possible to say what God is, as to essence,) but everywhere he declares Him to us by His workings. For this Word one may see shortly after called Light, and the Light in turn named Life.
florilegium.gloss: Chrysostom reads the Evangelist himself as working by this rule. St John never names the essence, and instead gives us the workings: Word, Light, Life. The whole prologue is an exercise in naming God from what he does.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: Shining upon those that are cleansed from every spot, He makes them spiritual by fellowship with Himself. Just as when a sunbeam falls on bright and transparent bodies, they themselves become brilliant too, and shed forth a fresh brightness from themselves, so souls wherein the Spirit dwells, illuminated by the Spirit, themselves become spiritual, and send forth their grace to others. Hence comes foreknowledge of the future, understanding of mysteries, apprehension of what is hidden, distribution of good gifts, the heavenly citizenship, a place in the chorus of angels, joy without end, abiding in God, the being made like to God, and, highest of all, the being made God.
florilegium.gloss: What the distinction is for. The list ends at the being made God, which is only sayable because what the Spirit gives is God himself and not a created gift. Basil's sunbeam is the standard patristic image for a giving that does not diminish the giver.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.text: It is plain, then, that there is a God. But what He is in His essence and nature is absolutely incomprehensible and unknowable.
florilegium.gloss: The Damascene states the two halves in two sentences. That God is, is plain. What he is in his essence, is not to be had by any creature.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.text: The Deity is simple and uncompound. But that which is composed of many and different elements is compound. If, then, we should speak of the qualities of being uncreate and without beginning and incorporeal and immortal and everlasting and good and creative and so forth as essential differences in the case of God, that which is composed of so many qualities will not be simple but must be compound. But this is impious in the extreme. Each then of the affirmations about God should be thought of as signifying not what He is in essence, but either something that it is impossible to make plain, or some relation to some of those things which are contrasts or some of those things that follow the nature, or an energy.
florilegium.gloss: The direct answer to the charge of composition, made by a Father who insists on simplicity as strongly as anyone. Precisely because God is uncompound, the things we affirm of him cannot all be read as essential differences. One of the categories the Damascene offers for them is energeia, which NPNF here renders energy.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.text: A man by counsel builds a house, but by nature he begets a son; and what is in building began to come into being at will, and is external to the maker; but the son is proper offspring of the father's essence, and is not external to him.
florilegium.gloss: Athanasius is arguing about the Son against the Arians, not about creation against anybody, and that is what makes the sentence useful. The distinction between what proceeds by nature and what is made by will is already load-bearing in the fourth century, and it is exactly the distinction the necessity problem needs.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.text: There being then much blasphemy in such a thought, it will be religious to say that things originate have come to be 'by favour and will,' but the Son is not a work of will, nor has come after, as the creation, but is by nature the own Offspring of God's Essence.
florilegium.gloss: The same rule stated as a formula. Creatures come to be by favour and will; the Son is of the essence by nature. Read against the necessity objection, it says that willing in God is not simply interchangeable with being God, or the creation would stand where the Son stands.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.text: But generation in Him is without beginning and everlasting, being the work of nature and producing out of His own essence, that the Begetter may not undergo change, and that He may not be God first and God last, nor receive any accession: while creation in the case of God, being the work of will, is not co-eternal with God. For it is not natural that that which is brought into existence out of nothing should be co-eternal with what is without beginning and everlasting.
florilegium.gloss: The conclusion the whole study has been walking toward, and it is stated by the Damascene without any polemical setting. Begetting is the work of nature and therefore eternal. Creation is the work of will and therefore not co-eternal. The world is a gift and not an overflow.

scripture.note: Moses asks to see the glory and is told that no man shall see the face of God and live, and is then shown the back parts. The Fathers take this as the whole doctrine in narrative form.
No man hath seen God at any time. The apostolic statement of the essence side, which the Church never softens.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. The apostolic statement of the other side, which the Church never softens either.
Dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto. Approachable light and unapproachable God, held together in one verse.
The invisible things of him are understood by the things that are made. St Basil's order of knowledge, from the operations to the knowledge of God, in a single line of St Paul.
Partakers of the divine nature. The verse the whole distinction exists to protect, since participation in the essence is impossible and participation in nothing is no participation.
The Transfiguration. His face did shine as the sun, seen by human eyes on a mountain, which is the case the hesychast controversy turned on.
The glory which thou gavest me I have given them. Glory is spoken of as given, not merely displayed.
For thy pleasure they are and were created. Creation is referred to God's good pleasure, which is the language St Athanasius uses for what comes to be by will.
Who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. Counsel and will are ascribed to God in his dealings with creatures, which is the vocabulary the necessity objection has to account for.
